planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Arp is among the most cold-hardy rosemary cultivars available, tolerating winter temperatures well below what kills most other rosemary.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Arp was discovered growing outdoors through winter in Arp, Texas, and remains one of the most reliably cold-hardy rosemary selections for gardeners north of the mild-winter regions where most rosemary is grown, surviving temperatures that kill standard culinary rosemary outright. Its upright, shrubby habit and lighter, grayer-green needle-like leaves have a milder flavor than some other culinary types, but it is still fully usable in cooking, and the plant produces pale blue flowers in spring. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain a full, bushy shape, and avoid heavy, wet, or poorly drained soil, which is a far greater threat to rosemary survival than cold in most gardens.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Salem is a cold-hardy selection that tolerates colder winters than standard culinary rosemary while keeping strong, classic flavor.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Salem is a compact, upright rosemary selected for good cold hardiness alongside strong, classic culinary flavor, making it a reliable choice for cooks in climates where standard rosemary cultivars struggle to overwinter outdoors. Pale blue-lavender flowers appear in spring on a tidy, dense, shrubby plant, and regular harvesting throughout the growing season encourages fuller, bushier growth. Prune lightly after flowering to keep the plant shapely, and give it sharply drained soil, since standing water in winter is a far greater threat to rosemary than cold temperatures alone.

planting.note: Root cuttings or plant divisions in spring in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Elfin forms an extremely dense, tight, low mat and is popular for miniature and fairy gardens as well as between stepping stones.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Elfin is among the smallest and slowest-growing thyme cultivars available, forming a dense, tightly cushioned mat of tiny leaves only an inch or two tall, far more compact than standard creeping thyme, which makes it a favorite for miniature gardens, trough plantings, and tucking between small paving stones where a larger thyme would quickly overwhelm the space. Small pale pink flowers appear in a light early-summer bloom above the foliage mat, drawing bees. Like other thymes it demands sharp drainage and resents wet feet, especially in winter; light foot traffic is fine on an established planting, releasing a mild fragrance when stepped on.

common_name: Hot and Spicy Oregano (Intensely Flavored Culinary Oregano)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery transplants after last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Hot and Spicy is grown for its notably intense, peppery-hot flavor, considerably stronger than standard culinary oregano.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun. Hot and Spicy was selected specifically for a much stronger, more peppery-hot flavor and aroma than typical culinary oregano, making it useful where a smaller quantity delivers a bigger flavor punch in sauces, pizza, and Mediterranean dishes. It forms a bushy, spreading clump of small, dark green, rounded leaves and produces small white to pale pink flowers in summer if left unharvested, though frequent picking for kitchen use keeps the plant compact and encourages fresh new growth. Like other oreganos it thrives on neglect once established, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil far better than rich, consistently moist conditions, which tend to dilute flavor and encourage floppy growth.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery transplants after last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Tricolor is less cold-hardy than plain culinary sage and benefits from winter mulch or container culture in colder zones.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun. Tricolor is grown as much for ornamental value as for the kitchen, with soft, gray-green leaves irregularly splashed in cream and edged in rosy purple-pink, especially vivid on new growth, giving the plant a decorative look that stands out in an herb border or mixed container far more than plain culinary sage. The leaves are fully usable in cooking with the same flavor as green sage, though the plant is generally somewhat less vigorous and less cold-hardy than the species, so it benefits from winter protection or container culture where winters are severe. Harvest leaves as needed through the growing season, and cut the plant back by about a third in spring to remove winter dieback and encourage fresh, well-colored new growth.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings under high humidity or plant container specimens in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade after frost; White Anne requires the highest consistent humidity of virtually any common tropical foliage plant and is ideally suited to terrariums and glass enclosures.

directions: Root stem cuttings or plant specimens in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full shade. White Anne carries a dense, intricate network of nearly pure white veins over darker green leaf tissue, a higher-contrast, more brightly patterned selection than the plain species, which shows more muted white-green veining. Like other nerve plants it fails quickly in dry household air and performs best in a terrarium, bottle garden, or humidity dome that maintains consistently high moisture around the foliage; leaves wilt dramatically at the first sign of dryness but usually recover within hours once watered, an easy visual cue for when to water. Pinch growing tips regularly to keep the low, creeping mat dense and full rather than sparse and leggy.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant, terrarium plant, or shaded hanging basket in bright indirect light in consistently moist, well-drained potting mix; Pilea depressa is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained potting mix, in a hanging basket, terrarium, or as a groundcover in a shaded container planting. Pilea depressa forms dense mats of tiny, rounded, bright green leaves on trailing stems that root readily wherever they touch soil, giving it a soft, mossy, cascading texture useful for softening the edge of a pot or covering the base of a taller terrarium planting. It is easy to propagate from stem cuttings and grows quickly in the right conditions, tolerating average indoor humidity better than many true miniature terrarium plants. Keep soil evenly moist but not waterlogged, and pinch stems to encourage denser, fuller growth rather than long, sparse trailers.
